Neonatal American flamingos emerge from eggs incubated for approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days] at a consistent temperature of 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C], with reports ranging from 28 to 32 days depending on local microclimatic conditions. Upon hatching, these semi-precocial chicks weigh roughly 94 grams [Wwb = roughly 94 grams], though field measurements indicate a normal span of 85 to 102 grams for this initial wet weight. This modest birth mass is typical among large wading birds and reflects the substantial energetic investment in a calcareous egg that must sustain embryonic development throughout the incubation period. The tightly regulated nest temperature achieved through attentive biparental brooding ensures that the gastrulating embryo develops within a narrow thermal window, optimizing developmental rates and hatchling viability. Newly hatched individuals are covered in white down and begin receiving a lipid-rich crop milk secretion from both parents within hours of hatching, a resource that fuels rapid early growth.

The developmental trajectory of the downy chick is notably rapid, with fledging—the achievement of first flight and the point at which young join the nursery creche—occurring at just 11 days after hatching [tx = 11 days after hatching] under the species' typical active-phase body temperature of 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C]. This remarkably short interval to joining the creche is an adaptation that reduces predation risk on individual nests. During this brief nestling period, the pin-feathered chick undergoes substantial mass gain, transitioning from the hatchling mass to a more robust form. The creching behavior itself serves multiple functions, including thermoregulatory benefits through huddling and collective vigilance against aerial predators. Adult flamingos continue to provision their own young within the creche through a system of individual recognition, and parental care remains intensive for several weeks thereafter.

Sexual maturation, or the attainment of puberty, is estimated to occur at approximately 33 days after hatching [tp = approximately 33 days after hatching] when maintained at the species' core body temperature of 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C]. This remarkably early onset of gonadal development in a long-lived bird species reflects the rapid somatic growth facilitated by energy-rich filter-feeding on brine shrimp and algae. However, reaching physiological puberty does not translate immediately into reproductive activity; first breeding, the time since birth at first brood, is considerably deferred. The initiation of reproductive effort typically occurs at approximately 3 years after hatching [tR = approximately 3 years after hatching] at 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], a delay consistent with observations in many colonially nesting waterbirds where social factors, including territory acquisition and pair bond formation, constrain early reproduction.

Adult body mass exhibits sexual dimorphism in the American flamingo, with males attaining a larger ultimate wet weight. While females generally reach a maximum adult mass of approximately 2200 grams [Wwi = approximately 2200 grams], males are substantially heavier, achieving an ultimate wet weight of about 2800 grams [Wwi = about 2800 grams]. This dimorphism is likely linked to male-male competition for breeding territories and nesting sites within dense colonies. In terms of reproductive output, females produce a single egg per breeding attempt [N_R_i = single egg per breeding attempt], and typically have only one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], representing a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 1 chick per year [Ri = approximately 1 chick per year] constrained by the high energetic demands of egg production and chick rearing. The species exhibits a maximum documented lifespan in the wild of approximately 44 years [am = approximately 44 years] when measured at the typical active body temperature of 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], placing it among the most long-lived of all wading birds.

The remarkable longevity of the American flamingo, with individuals surviving up to 44 years [am = up to 44 years] under optimal conditions at 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], is accompanied by a slow life-history pace characterized by deferred reproduction and low annual fecundity. The single-egg clutch [N_R_i = single-egg clutch] and annual breeding frequency [F_R_i = annual breeding frequency] together produce a low maximum reproductive output that is typical of species investing heavily in individual offspring survival. The delayed age at first breeding, approximately 3 years after hatching [tR = approximately 3 years after hatching] at 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], further exemplifies this conservative strategy. As they age, adults undergo reproductive senescence, but their long reproductive lifespan allows for many breeding seasons. The same core body temperature of 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C] that facilitates rapid fledging at 11 days [tx = 11 days] and early puberty at 33 days [tp = 33 days] also supports the metabolic demands of such an extended life, balancing developmental pace with durable physiological maintenance.
